newsitem.title: USA: Stocks, dollar fall, bonds little changed.
newsitem.headline: Stocks, dollar fall, bonds little changed.

text.p: Stocks fell sharply Tuesday as a strong housing report reignited fears the Federal Reserve would raise interest rates in a bid to ward off inflation.
The dollar fell on fresh concerns about Europe's planned single currency.
Oil and gold edged higher. Bonds ended little changed.

The Dow Jones industrial average lost 58.92 points to 6,896.56 after falling 100 points earlier in the session. In the broader market, declining issues beat advances 1,643 to 844 on volume of 467 million shares on the New York Stock Exchange.

A government report that housing starts rose 12.2 percent in February to the fastest rate in nearly three years further worried investors that Fed policy-makers would raise short-term rates at their meeting on March 25 to slow the economy's growth.
While the jump in housing starts was aided by unusually warm weather, the robust activity still surprised economists.
"Even adjusting for seasonal flukiness, the housing sector is doing extremely well," said David Wyss, an economist at DRI/McGraw Hill Inc.
"This market is obsessed with March 25," said Jack Shaughnessy, director of research at Advest. "The strong housing numbers this morning contributed to that."
He said the stock market appeared prepared for a marginal increase of a quarter point in short-term rates, but "there's a fear there might be even more of an increase."
Higher interest rates would hurt corporate profits and thus, stock prices.
With several major reports to come before the meeting of central bank policy-makers, analysts said volatility was only going to increase in the days ahead.

"We've got the (Consumer Price Index) tomorrow, triple witching on Friday and the Fed next week," said Alfred Goldman, technical analyst at A.G. Edwards & Sons. "Until the Fed drops the other shoe or puts it back on its foot, this market is going to stay whippy."
In currency trading, the dollar fell sharply as the mark rallied after a German central banker spoke of a postponement in Europe's planned single currency.
The dollar fell to 1.6730 marks late in New York from 1.6910 late on Monday. It declined to 122.43 Japanese yen from 123.74 yen and to 1.4385 Swiss francs from 1.4590 Swiss.

The mark extended recent gains against the British pound and other European currencies after Bundesbank council member Klaus-Dieter Kuehbacher joined a number of German officials this week who seemed to throw cold water on the plan to merge Europe's currencies in 1999.

"It's a broad-based dollar sale, in combination with a broad-based advance of the deutschemark against its major trading partners," said John Nelson, foreign exchange trading manager at ABN-AMRO Bank.

In an interview with "Boerse Online" magazine published Tuesday, Kuebacher said the single currency might have to be delayed because he saw little chance that Germany would be able to reduce its government deficit enough to meet key conditions for joining the single currency plan.
In the bond market, the 30-year Treasury ended with its yield unchanged at 6.96 percent.

Oil prices rose on concerns that a barge accident on the Mississippi River could slow oil shipments headed north. Crude oil for April delivery rose $1.14 to $22.06 a barrel at the New York Mercantile Exchange.
April gold added $2.10 to $350.40 an ounce at New York's Commodity Exchange.
Overseas, London's FTSE 100 index lost 16.5 points to 4,356.8 and Tokyo's 225-share Nikkei average gained 391.70 points to 18,445.20.
